decks.title: Tissues, Part 1: levels of organisation and plant tissues
goals: Describe the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism
Distinguish meristematic and permanent plant tissues and name their types
Relate the structure of parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem, phloem and epidermis to their function
Find the actual size of a cell from a drawing

slides.heading: Tissues: teams of cells
slides.body_md: Part 1: how cells are organised, and the tissues that build a plant.

rows: A palisade cell of a leaf

visual.alt: Table of the five levels of organisation with a plant and an animal example for each

slides.narration: A single cell can do everything, but a tree or a cow needs far more. So cells work in teams, and the teams are arranged in levels. A group of similar cells doing one job is a tissue. Tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and the systems together make the organism. In this part we meet the levels of organisation, and then the tissues of plants.

slides.heading: Levels of organisation
slides.body_md: In a multicellular organism, cells are grouped into **tissues**, tissues into **organs**, organs into **organ systems**. This is **division of labour**: each level does a job that no single cell could do well.

visual.alt: Flow from cell to tissue, organ, organ system and organism

slides.narration: Look at the levels. Cells of the same kind form a tissue. Several tissues join to form an organ, such as a leaf or a heart. Organs that work together form an organ system, such as the digestive system. All the systems together make a whole organism. This is called division of labour, because every level does a job that a single cell could not do well.

slides.heading: Why tissues are useful
slides.body_md: A tissue is a group of cells with the **same structure** that do a **particular job**. Because cells specialise, the organism works more efficiently.

visual.alt: Table of three tissues, the shape of their cells and their jobs

slides.narration: A tissue is a group of cells that have the same structure and carry out one particular job. The shape of the cells suits the job. Xylem cells form hollow tubes that carry water up a tree. Muscle cells are long fibres that can shorten. Epidermis cells are flat and tightly packed, so they protect the leaf. Specialisation makes the whole organism work better.

slides.heading: Two groups of plant tissue
slides.body_md: Plant tissues are of two groups: **meristematic** tissues, which divide and make the plant grow, and **permanent** tissues, whose cells have taken a fixed shape and job.

visual.alt: Tree diagram of plant tissues into meristematic and permanent, with the types of permanent tissue

slides.narration: Plants grow in particular regions, and that is because of meristematic tissue. Its cells keep dividing. Cells made by meristems become permanent tissue, and then they stop dividing and take up a particular shape and job. Permanent tissue is simple, such as parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, or complex, such as xylem and phloem, or protective, such as epidermis and cork.

slides.heading: Meristematic tissue
slides.body_md: Meristematic cells are **small, thin-walled, closely packed**, with dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus and no large vacuole. They divide again and again. **Apical** meristems at tips add length, **lateral** meristems (cambium) add girth, and **intercalary** meristems at the base of leaves or internodes add length where it is needed.

slides.narration: Meristematic cells are small, thin-walled and packed closely, with dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus. They divide again and again. The apical meristem at the tip of a root or shoot makes the plant longer. The lateral meristem, called cambium, makes a stem or root thicker. The intercalary meristem, at the base of a leaf or an internode, adds length, which is why grass regrows after grazing.

slides.heading: Worked example: which meristem?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the meristem responsible for each observation. (a) A lawn on a cricket ground grows back after mowing. (b) The trunk of a neem tree gets thicker every year. (c) The root of a bean seedling gets longer.

**Step 1.** Ask: is the growth in length or in thickness, and where does it happen?

**(a)** Length, at the base of the leaves, below the cut: **intercalary** meristem.

**(b)** Thickness: **lateral** meristem (cambium).

**(c)** Length, at the root tip: **apical** meristem.

visual.alt: Table linking three observations to the meristem responsible

slides.narration: Let us find the meristem for each case. The lawn grows back after mowing because the cells at the base of the leaves keep dividing, which is intercalary meristem. A neem trunk grows thicker because of the lateral meristem, called cambium. A bean seedling root grows longer because of the apical meristem at its tip. Always ask whether the growth is in length or thickness, and where it happens.

slides.heading: Simple permanent tissues
slides.body_md: Simple permanent tissues are made of one kind of cell. **Parenchyma** has thin-walled living cells, **collenchyma** has living cells with thickened corners, and **sclerenchyma** has dead cells with thick lignified walls.

slides.narration: Simple permanent tissues have only one kind of cell. Parenchyma cells are thin-walled, living and loosely packed, and they store food. Collenchyma cells have thickened corners, which gives flexible support, as in the strings of celery. Sclerenchyma cells are dead, with thick hard walls, and they give strength, as in the husk of a coconut or the shell of a nut.

slides.heading: Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma compared
slides.body_md: Variants of parenchyma: **chlorenchyma** has chloroplasts and makes food; **aerenchyma** has large air spaces and helps aquatic plants float.

rows: Stores food; chlorenchyma makes food; aerenchyma floats aquatic plants

visual.alt: Table of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma with their cells, places and jobs

slides.narration: Compare the three tissues. Parenchyma is found in a potato tuber, in leaves and in the pith of stems. With chloroplasts it is called chlorenchyma and makes food. With large air spaces, as in water plants, it is called aerenchyma and helps the plant float. Collenchyma is found in leaf stalks and young stems. Sclerenchyma is found in coconut husk and seed coats, and its cells are dead.

slides.narration: Complex tissues are made of more than one kind of cell. Xylem has tracheids and vessels, which are hollow tubes of dead cells with thick walls, along with fibres and parenchyma. Xylem carries water and minerals upwards. Phloem has sieve tubes, whose end walls have holes, and companion cells. Phloem carries the food made in leaves to all parts, both upwards and downwards.

slides.heading: Xylem and phloem compared
slides.body_md: Xylem is mostly dead and its main role is transport and support. Phloem is mostly living and needs its companion cells to work.

rows: Sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres, parenchyma

visual.alt: Table comparing xylem and phloem

slides.narration: Here is the comparison. Xylem carries water and minerals, and only upwards. Its main parts are vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma, and most of it is dead. Phloem carries food made in leaves, upwards and downwards. Its main parts are sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma, and most of it is living. A good exam answer lists a few of these points.

slides.body_md: Decide which tissue is meant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask what is being carried, and in which direction, to decide between xylem and phloem.

slides.heading: Protective tissue: epidermis and cork
slides.body_md: The **epidermis** is usually a single layer of tightly packed cells. In leaves it has pores called **stomata**, each guarded by two **guard cells**, and a waxy **cuticle**. Older stems have **cork**, dead cells with a waterproof coating.

rows: Gas exchange and loss of water vapour

visual.alt: Table of protective tissues of plants with their features and jobs

slides.narration: Protective tissue covers the plant. The epidermis is usually one layer of tightly packed cells. In leaves it has a waxy coat that reduces loss of water, and it has tiny pores called stomata, each between two guard cells, for exchange of gases. In roots, epidermal cells form root hairs that absorb water. Older stems are covered by cork, which is made of dead cells.

slides.heading: Worked example: size of a vessel
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student draws a xylem vessel seen under a microscope. The drawing is 15 mm wide and the magnification is 250 times. Find the actual width of the vessel in micrometres.

**Step 1.** Actual size $= \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{magnification}} = \dfrac{15\ \text{mm}}{250} = 0.06\ \text{mm}$.

**Step 2.** $0.06\ \text{mm} \times 1000 = 60\ \mu\text{m}$.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for finding actual size from a drawing

slides.narration: Here is a short calculation. The drawing of a xylem vessel is fifteen millimetres wide, and the magnification is two hundred and fifty. Divide the drawing size by the magnification to get the actual width in millimetres. Then multiply by one thousand to change it to micrometres. The result is sixty micrometres, which is thinner than a human hair.

bullets: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and these form the organism.

Simple permanent: parenchyma (stores, makes food), collenchyma (flexible support), sclerenchyma (strength, dead).
Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries food both ways.
Epidermis protects; stomata exchange gases; cork covers older stems.

visual.alt: Summary table of plant tissues and their jobs

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Cells are organised into tissues, organs and organ systems. Meristematic tissue divides, with apical and intercalary meristems adding length and lateral meristem adding thickness. Permanent tissues are simple, complex or protective. Xylem carries water and minerals upwards, and phloem carries food in both directions. In Part 2 we turn to animal tissues.

slides.heading: Animal tissues
slides.body_md: Part 2: the four tissues of animals, the joints that let us move, and how to look after them.

visual.alt: Table of four animal tissues with an example from the human body

slides.narration: Your body is a team of trillions of cells, working as four main kinds of tissue. Epithelial tissue covers and lines. Connective tissue supports and joins, and includes blood and bone. Muscular tissue moves the body, and nervous tissue carries signals. In this part we look at each, then at the joints that let you move, and at how to care for your bones and muscles.

slides.heading: The four animal tissues
slides.body_md: Animal tissues are **epithelial**, **connective**, **muscular** and **nervous**. Unlike plants, animals grow all over the body, so they have no separate meristems.

visual.alt: Tree diagram of the four animal tissues and the job of each

slides.narration: Animals have four kinds of tissue. Epithelial tissue covers surfaces and lines hollow organs. Connective tissue supports the body and joins other tissues together. Muscular tissue contracts to produce movement. Nervous tissue carries signals quickly from one part of the body to another. Animals grow all over the body, so unlike plants they have no separate meristems.

slides.heading: Epithelial tissue
slides.body_md: Epithelial cells are **tightly packed** with very little space between them. They sit on a **basement membrane**. They form the skin, and line the mouth, blood vessels, kidney tubules, intestine and windpipe.

slides.narration: Epithelial tissue forms a covering or a lining. Its cells are tightly packed with almost no space between them, and they rest on a basement membrane. Squamous cells are flat, cuboidal cells are cube-shaped, and columnar cells are tall. In the windpipe, columnar cells carry tiny hair-like cilia that sweep out mucus and dust. Glandular epithelium makes secretions such as sweat and saliva.

slides.heading: Types of epithelium and their jobs
slides.body_md: Structure matches function: thin flat cells allow easy exchange, tall cells have room for absorption and secretion.

rows: Lining of mouth, blood vessels, skin surface

visual.alt: Table of epithelial tissue types with where they occur and their jobs

slides.narration: Here are the types. Squamous epithelium lines the mouth and blood vessels, where its thin flat cells protect and let substances pass easily. Cuboidal epithelium forms kidney tubules and gland ducts. Columnar epithelium lines the small intestine and absorbs food. Ciliated columnar epithelium in the windpipe moves mucus. Glandular epithelium makes secretions, for example in salivary and sweat glands.

slides.body_md: Connective cells are **scattered in a matrix**, which may be liquid, jelly-like, firm or hard. Connective tissue supports, joins, stores, transports and protects.

slides.narration: Connective tissue has cells scattered in a matrix, a material they make themselves. In blood the matrix is liquid plasma. In bone it is hard, with calcium and phosphorus salts. In cartilage it is firm and flexible. Tendons and ligaments are dense bands of strong fibres. A tendon joins muscle to bone, while a ligament joins one bone to another.

slides.heading: Kinds of connective tissue
slides.body_md: Blood has three kinds of cells in plasma: **red blood cells** carry oxygen, **white blood cells** fight germs, and **platelets** help blood to clot.

rows: Hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus salts
Smooth surfaces at joints; shapes ear and nose

visual.alt: Table of seven connective tissues with their features and jobs

slides.narration: Here are seven connective tissues. Areolar tissue fills the spaces inside organs and helps in repair. Adipose tissue stores fat. Blood transports oxygen, food and wastes, and defends against germs. Bone supports and protects. Cartilage is firm but flexible, as in the ear and the nose. A ligament joins bone to bone, and a tendon joins muscle to bone.

slides.heading: Worked example: name the tissue
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the tissue in each case. (a) A layer of tall cells lining the small intestine, where food is absorbed. (b) Strong cords joining the muscles of the calf to the heel bone. (c) Long cells that can send a signal over a metre.

**Step 1.** (a) Tall cells in a lining: **columnar epithelium**.

**Step 2.** (b) Muscle to bone: **tendon**, a connective tissue.

**Step 3.** (c) Signals over long distances: a **neuron**, nervous tissue.

visual.alt: Table linking three clues to the animal tissue they point to

slides.narration: Use the clues. Tall cells forming a lining in the small intestine are columnar epithelium. A strong cord joining calf muscle to the heel bone is a tendon, which is connective tissue. A long cell that carries a signal over a distance of a metre is a neuron, which is nervous tissue. Look for the shape of the cells and the job they do.

slides.heading: Muscular tissue
slides.body_md: Muscle cells contain fibres that **contract** and relax. **Striated** muscle is attached to bones and is voluntary. **Smooth** muscle is in the walls of the food pipe and blood vessels. **Cardiac** muscle is found only in the heart.

slides.narration: Muscle cells are long, and they contract and relax to produce movement. Striated, or skeletal, muscle has light and dark stripes and many nuclei, and we control it. Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus each and no stripes, and it works without our control, for example in the food pipe. Cardiac muscle is striped, branched and found only in the heart.

slides.heading: The three muscles compared
slides.body_md: **Voluntary** muscles work when we decide. **Involuntary** muscles work without our control.

visual.alt: Table comparing striated, smooth and cardiac muscle

slides.narration: Compare the muscles. Striated muscle has stripes, many nuclei, long unbranched fibres, and is voluntary, found in limbs and the body wall. Smooth muscle has no stripes, one nucleus and spindle-shaped cells, and is involuntary, found in the food pipe and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle has stripes, one nucleus and branched fibres, is involuntary, and is found only in the heart.

slides.narration: Nervous tissue is made of nerve cells, or neurons. Branched dendrites receive signals and pass them to the cell body, which holds the nucleus. The long axon carries the impulse away from the cell body, and its end splits into nerve endings that pass the signal on to the next cell. An axon in a human can be about a metre long, and nerves are bundles of such fibres.

slides.narration: Joints are the places where bones meet. A ball and socket joint, as at the shoulder and hip, allows movement in all directions. A hinge joint, as at the elbow and knee, moves back and forth in one plane. A pivot joint in the neck lets the head turn. Gliding joints at the wrist and ankle allow small sliding movements. Fixed joints in the skull allow no movement.

slides.heading: Caring for bones and muscles
slides.body_md: Good **posture**, regular **exercise** and a diet with **calcium** and **vitamin D** keep the musculoskeletal system healthy. Calcium builds bone and vitamin D helps the body absorb it.

Strengthens bones and muscles; keeps joints flexible
Milk, curd, ragi, sesame and green leafy vegetables
Some time in morning sunlight; egg yolk, fish
Skin makes vitamin D; helps absorb calcium

visual.alt: Table of habits for caring for bones and muscles and the reason for each

slides.narration: To keep bones and muscles healthy, sit and stand straight, and carry a school bag on both shoulders. Exercise every day by walking, running, playing and stretching. Eat foods rich in calcium, such as milk, curd, ragi and green leafy vegetables. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and the skin makes it in sunlight. Too little vitamin D in children can cause soft, bent bones.

slides.heading: Worked example: calcium in milk
slides.body_md:
**Problem (illustrative data).** A student needs about 1000 mg of calcium a day. Milk has about 120 mg in 100 mL. How many 200 mL glasses of milk would supply her whole need?

**Step 1.** Calcium in one glass $= 120 \times \dfrac{200}{100} = 240\ \text{mg}$.

**Step 2.** Glasses needed $= \dfrac{1000}{240} \approx 4.2$. In practice, about three to four glasses plus calcium from other foods such as ragi and green vegetables.

nodes.label: Divide daily need by one glass

visual.alt: Flow showing the steps for working out how many glasses of milk supply the daily calcium

slides.narration: Let us use some numbers. Suppose milk has about one hundred and twenty milligrams of calcium in every hundred millilitres. One glass of two hundred millilitres then gives two hundred and forty milligrams. If a student needs about one thousand milligrams a day, that is a little over four glasses. In practice she also gets calcium from other foods such as ragi, curd and green leafy vegetables.

Connective tissue has cells in a matrix: blood, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, areolar, adipose.
Striated, smooth and cardiac muscle contract to give movement.
The neuron has dendrites, cell body, axon and nerve endings.
Joints: ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, fixed. Posture, exercise, calcium and vitamin D protect bones and muscles.

Blood, bone, cartilage, tendon and ligament are connective tissues. Joints are of five kinds. Good posture, regular exercise and enough calcium and vitamin D keep bones and muscles strong throughout life.

sections.heading: 1. Levels of organisation
sections.body_md:
A multicellular organism is built in levels: **cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism**. A **tissue** is a group of cells with the same structure that do a particular job. An **organ** (leaf, root, heart, stomach) is made of several tissues. An **organ system** (digestive system, shoot system) is a group of organs working together. This division of labour makes the organism efficient.

Actual size from a drawing: $\text{actual size} = \dfrac{\text{size of drawing}}{\text{magnification}}$, and $1\ \text{mm} = 1000\ \mu\text{m}$.

A group of organs that work together, such as the digestive system.

sections.heading: 2. Meristematic tissue
sections.body_md:
**Meristematic** cells are small, thin-walled and closely packed, with dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus and no large vacuole. They divide again and again.

- **Apical meristem:** tips of roots and shoots; adds length.
- **Lateral meristem (cambium):** along the sides of stems and roots; adds girth.
- **Intercalary meristem:** at the base of leaves or internodes (as in grass); adds length and lets grass regrow after grazing.

Cells made by the meristems become **permanent** tissue.

key_terms.definition_md: A tissue whose cells keep dividing to make the plant grow.
The lateral meristem that makes stems and roots thicker.
The process by which new cells take up a fixed shape and job.

sections.heading: 3. Simple and complex permanent tissues of plants
sections.body_md:
**Simple permanent tissues:** parenchyma (living, thin-walled; stores food; chlorenchyma makes food; aerenchyma floats aquatic plants), collenchyma (living, corners thickened; flexible support) and sclerenchyma (dead, thick lignified walls; strength).

**Complex permanent tissues:** **xylem** (tracheids, vessels, fibres, parenchyma) carries water and minerals upwards; **phloem** (sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres, parenchyma) carries food both upwards and downwards.

Simple tissue of living cells with thickened corners that gives flexible support.
Simple tissue of dead cells with thick hard walls that gives strength.
Complex tissue that carries water and minerals upwards.
Complex tissue that carries food made in leaves to all parts.

sections.heading: 4. Protective tissue of plants
sections.body_md: The **epidermis** is usually one layer of tightly packed cells. In aerial parts it has a waxy **cuticle** that reduces water loss. **Stomata**, pores each between two **guard cells**, let gases and water vapour pass. In roots, epidermal cells make **root hairs** that absorb water. Older stems are covered by **cork**, dead cells with a waterproof coating that protect the stem.

key_terms.definition_md: Tiny pores in the epidermis, each between two guard cells, for exchange of gases.
A waxy layer on the outer wall of epidermal cells that reduces water loss.
Dead cells with a waterproof wall that cover the older stem.

sections.heading: 5. Animal tissues: epithelial and connective
sections.body_md:
**Epithelial tissue** has tightly packed cells on a basement membrane: squamous (flat; mouth, blood vessels, skin), cuboidal (kidney tubules), columnar (small intestine), ciliated columnar (windpipe) and glandular (sweat and salivary glands).

**Connective tissue** has cells scattered in a matrix. **Blood** (plasma with red cells, white cells and platelets), **bone** (hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus salts), **cartilage** (firm, flexible), **ligament** (joins bone to bone), **tendon** (joins muscle to bone), **areolar** (fills spaces) and **adipose** (stores fat).

key_terms.definition_md: Tissue of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces and lines organs.
The material between connective tissue cells; it may be liquid, firm or hard.
A strong cord of connective tissue that joins muscle to bone.
A strong, elastic band of connective tissue that joins bone to bone.

sections.heading: 6. Animal tissues: muscular and nervous
sections.body_md:
**Striated (skeletal)** muscle: stripes, many nuclei, long unbranched fibres, voluntary. **Smooth** muscle: no stripes, one nucleus, spindle-shaped, involuntary (food pipe, blood vessels). **Cardiac** muscle: stripes, one nucleus, branched, involuntary, in the heart only.

**Nervous tissue** is made of **neurons**. Dendrites receive signals, the cell body holds the nucleus, the axon carries the impulse away, and nerve endings pass it on. An axon can be about a metre long.

key_terms.definition_md: Muscle that we can control, such as the muscles of the arm.
Muscle that works without our control, such as heart muscle.
A nerve cell with dendrites, a cell body, an axon and nerve endings.

sections.heading: 7. Joints and care of the musculoskeletal system
sections.body_md:
**Joints:** ball and socket (shoulder, hip; all directions), hinge (elbow, knee; one plane), pivot (neck; rotation), gliding (wrist, ankle; sliding) and fixed (skull; no movement). Ligaments hold the bones and cartilage cushions the ends.

**Care:** keep good posture, exercise regularly, and eat food with **calcium** (milk, curd, ragi, sesame, green leafy vegetables). **Vitamin D** (from sunlight, egg yolk and fish) helps the body absorb calcium. Too little vitamin D in children can cause soft, bent bones (rickets).

key_terms.definition_md: A place where two bones meet.
The way the body is held when sitting, standing or moving.
A vitamin that helps the body absorb calcium for bones.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that phloem carries water, or that xylem carries food.
- Saying that sclerenchyma is living.
- Mixing up tendon (muscle to bone) and ligament (bone to bone).
- Calling cardiac muscle voluntary, or smooth muscle striped.
- Writing that vitamin D builds bone instead of helping calcium absorption.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a name, a place or one function.
- 2-mark items: two points, one mark each.
- 3-mark items: three short, correct points with an example.
- 5-mark items: a neat labelled diagram (about 2 marks) and a clear comparison or description.

cards.front_md: List the levels of organisation in a multicellular organism.
cards.back_md: Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.

cards.front_md: What is a tissue?
cards.back_md: A group of cells with the same structure that carry out a particular job.

cards.front_md: Name the two main groups of plant tissue.
cards.back_md: Meristematic and permanent.

cards.front_md: What are three features of meristematic cells?
cards.back_md: Small, thin-walled and closely packed, with dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus.

cards.front_md: Where is the apical meristem and what does it do?
cards.back_md: At the tips of roots and shoots; adds length.

cards.front_md: What is the job of the lateral meristem?
cards.back_md: It makes stems and roots thicker (cambium).

cards.front_md: Why does grass regrow after being grazed?
cards.back_md: The intercalary meristem at the base of the leaves keeps dividing.

cards.front_md: Name the three simple permanent tissues.
cards.back_md: Parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma.

cards.front_md: What is chlorenchyma?
cards.back_md: Parenchyma that contains chloroplasts and makes food.

cards.front_md: What is aerenchyma and where is it found?
cards.back_md: Parenchyma with large air spaces, found in aquatic plants; helps them float.

cards.front_md: Which plant tissue has thickened corners and gives flexible support?
cards.back_md: Collenchyma, as in the strings of celery.

cards.front_md: Why is sclerenchyma strong?
cards.back_md: Its dead cells have very thick, hard, lignified walls.

cards.front_md: What does xylem carry, and in which direction?
cards.back_md: Water and minerals, upwards.

cards.front_md: What does phloem carry, and in which direction?
cards.back_md: Food made in the leaves, upwards and downwards.

cards.front_md: Name the parts of phloem.
cards.back_md: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma.

cards.front_md: What are stomata?
cards.back_md: Tiny pores in the epidermis, each between two guard cells, for exchange of gases.

cards.front_md: What is cork?
cards.back_md: Dead cells with a waterproof wall that protect older stems.

cards.front_md: Two features of epithelial tissue?
cards.back_md: Tightly packed cells, resting on a basement membrane.

cards.front_md: Where is ciliated columnar epithelium found?
cards.back_md: In the windpipe, where cilia sweep mucus and dust out.

cards.front_md: What is the matrix of blood?
cards.back_md: Liquid plasma.

cards.front_md: What does a tendon join? A ligament?
cards.back_md: Tendon: muscle to bone. Ligament: bone to bone.

cards.front_md: What makes bone hard?
cards.back_md: Calcium and phosphorus salts in its matrix.

cards.front_md: Where do you find cartilage?
cards.back_md: Ear, nose, windpipe rings and the ends of bones at joints.

cards.front_md: Three kinds of cell in blood and their jobs?
cards.back_md: Red cells carry oxygen; white cells fight germs; platelets help clotting.

cards.front_md: Striated muscle: stripes, nuclei, control?
cards.back_md: Stripes, many nuclei, voluntary.

cards.front_md: Smooth muscle: stripes, nuclei, where?
cards.back_md: No stripes, one nucleus, spindle-shaped; in food pipe and blood vessels.

cards.front_md: Where is cardiac muscle found and is it voluntary?
cards.back_md: Only in the heart; involuntary.

cards.front_md: Name the parts of a neuron.
cards.back_md: Dendrites, cell body, axon, nerve endings.

cards.front_md: Name five types of joint with one example each.
cards.back_md: Ball and socket (hip), hinge (knee), pivot (neck), gliding (wrist), fixed (skull).

cards.front_md: How do calcium and vitamin D help bones?
cards.back_md: Calcium builds bone; vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.

cards.front_md: Name two daily habits that protect bones and muscles.
cards.back_md: Good posture, and regular exercise.

questions.stem_md: A banyan leaf is made of epidermis, parenchyma, xylem and phloem working together. At which level of organisation is the leaf?
questions.solution_md: A leaf is made of several tissues that work together for photosynthesis, so it is an organ — option (b). Each separate tissue, such as xylem, would be one level lower, and the whole shoot would be an organ system.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the levels of organisation of a cow from the smallest to the largest, giving an example for each level except the organism. Why is this arrangement useful?

answer.model_answer_md: The order is cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism. For example, a muscle cell forms muscular tissue, muscles and the heart are organs, and the circulatory system is an organ system that belongs to the cow. This division of labour is useful because each level does a job that a single cell could not do well.

questions.solution_md: Five levels with examples; division of labour.

marking_scheme.step: Five levels in the right order
A correct example for at least three levels
Division of labour makes the organism efficient

questions.stem_md: True or false? The stomach is an organ, and the digestive system, which includes the stomach, is an organ system.
questions.solution_md: True. The stomach is made of several tissues working together, and organs such as the stomach, intestine and liver together form the digestive system.

questions.stem_md: Several different tissues working together to do a job, as in a root or a heart, form an ______.
questions.solution_md: Tissues combine to form an organ, and organs combine to form an organ system.

questions.stem_md: Is a mango leaf a cell, a tissue or an organ? Give one reason, and say how the many tissues in it show division of labour.

answer.model_answer_md: A mango leaf is an organ, because it is made of several tissues working together. The epidermis protects it, the parenchyma makes food, and the xylem and phloem carry water and food, so each tissue does a separate job.

questions.solution_md: Organ; epidermis, parenchyma and vessels each do one job.

marking_scheme.step: Organ, because it has several tissues

questions.stem_md: A bamboo shoot grows several centimetres longer in a night, mainly from the lower part of each segment between two nodes. Which tissue is responsible for this growth?
questions.solution_md: Growth at the base of an internode is the work of the intercalary meristem — option (c). The lateral meristem adds thickness, and sclerenchyma is dead tissue that cannot divide.

questions.stem_md: The strings in a celery stalk let it bend without snapping. Which tissue gives this flexible support?
questions.solution_md: Collenchyma has living cells with thickened corners and gives flexible support, so the stalk can bend — option (d). Sclerenchyma is hard and rigid, and aerenchyma has air spaces.

questions.stem_md: A gardener sees that a branch cut from a tree wilts quickly, even though it is in the shade. Which tissue has stopped supplying the leaves with water?
questions.solution_md: Water and minerals move upwards through xylem, and cutting the branch breaks that supply — option (d). Phloem carries food, not water.

questions.stem_md: A herd of goats grazes a field of grass, but the grass grows back within a week. Which statement explains this best?

options.text_md: Dividing cells at the base of the leaves are not removed when the tips are eaten.
The apical meristem of the root pushes the leaves up again.
The lateral meristem makes the blades longer.

questions.solution_md: Intercalary meristem at the base of the leaves lies below the part that is eaten, so it keeps dividing and the leaves lengthen again — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The stem of a lotus has large air spaces between its cells. This tissue helps the plant to:

options.text_md: float and exchange gases in water

questions.solution_md: A parenchyma with large air spaces is called aerenchyma. The air gives buoyancy, so the plant floats and gets gases — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A forest officer counts the rings in a tree trunk and finds that the trunk of a sal tree has become much wider over 40 years. The widening is due to:

options.text_md: apical meristem at the shoot tip
lateral meristem that makes new xylem and phloem
cork cells dividing in the leaves

questions.solution_md: Increase in girth is the work of the lateral meristem, the cambium, which adds new xylem and phloem each year — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The tough fibres of a coconut husk are used to make ropes and doormats. They are made of:

options.text_md: sclerenchyma, whose dead cells have thick lignified walls
collenchyma, whose living cells have thick corners
phloem, whose sieve tubes carry food

questions.solution_md: Husk fibres are sclerenchyma: dead cells with thick hard walls that give great strength — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sugar made in the leaves of a sugarcane plant reaches the stem, the roots and the growing tip. The tissue that carries it is:

options.text_md: phloem, which carries food both upwards and downwards
xylem, which carries food only upwards
phloem, which carries food only downwards
xylem, which carries food in both directions

questions.solution_md: Phloem carries the food made in leaves to all parts, upwards and downwards — option (a). Xylem carries water and minerals upwards.

questions.stem_md: A white tuberose flower is kept for a day in a bottle of red ink diluted with water. Thin red lines appear in its petals. These lines show the position of:

options.text_md: phloem, which carries the coloured water
xylem, which carries the coloured water

questions.solution_md: The coloured water is taken up through the stem and carried upwards by xylem, so the red lines mark xylem — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Meristematic cells are living and divide actively.

**Reason (R):** Meristematic cells have a large central vacuole and very thick walls.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Meristematic cells are living and keep dividing, so A is true. They are small and thin-walled with dense cytoplasm and no large vacuole, so R is false — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Xylem can carry water to the top of a tall tree even though most of its cells are dead.

**Reason (R):** The dead xylem vessels are hollow tubes with thick walls and no end walls, so water can pass through them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Vessels are empty tubes of dead cells, so water passes through them without any need for living contents. R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Cells of sclerenchyma are alive and keep dividing to repair a damaged stem.
questions.solution_md: False. Sclerenchyma cells are dead, with thick lignified walls, and permanent tissue does not divide.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The waxy cuticle on the outer wall of a leaf epidermis helps the leaf to lose less water.
questions.solution_md: True. The wax is waterproof, so it reduces loss of water from the surface of the leaf.

questions.stem_md: The tissue that carries water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards; phloem carries food.

questions.stem_md: Each stoma in the epidermis of a leaf is surrounded by two ______ cells.
questions.solution_md: A pair of guard cells surrounds each stoma and controls its opening.

questions.stem_md: Match each plant tissue (column I) with its role or place (column II).

match_right.text_md: Makes the husk of a coconut tough
Stores starch in a potato tuber
Carries sugar from leaves to roots
Lets a leaf stalk bend without breaking

questions.solution_md: Parenchyma stores starch; collenchyma gives flexible support; sclerenchyma gives hardness; phloem carries food.

questions.stem_md: A drawing of a xylem vessel is 17 mm wide and the magnification is 500. Find the actual width of the vessel in micrometres.
questions.solution_md: Actual width $= \dfrac{17\ \text{mm}}{500} = 0.034\ \text{mm}$. Converting, $0.034 \times 1000 = 34\ \mu\text{m}$.

marking_scheme.step: Divides drawing size by the magnification: 0.034 mm

questions.stem_md: State one difference between the apical meristem and the lateral meristem in position and in the growth they cause.

answer.model_answer_md: The apical meristem lies at the tips of roots and shoots and makes the plant longer. The lateral meristem, the cambium, lies along the sides of stems and roots and makes them thicker.

questions.solution_md: Tips and length against sides and girth.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between xylem and phloem.

answer.model_answer_md: Xylem carries water and minerals upwards from the roots, whereas phloem carries food made in the leaves upwards and downwards. Most xylem is made of dead cells, whereas most phloem is made of living cells such as sieve tubes and companion cells.

questions.solution_md: What is carried and direction; dead against living.

marking_scheme.step: Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries food both ways
Xylem mostly dead cells; phloem mostly living cells

questions.stem_md: A desert plant has a thick waxy coat and few stomata on its leaves. Explain how each feature helps it to survive.

answer.model_answer_md: The thick waxy cuticle forms a waterproof layer that cuts down the loss of water from the surface of the leaf. Stomata are the pores through which water vapour escapes, so having few of them further reduces water loss while still allowing some exchange of gases.

questions.solution_md: Cuticle reduces water loss; few stomata reduce evaporation.

marking_scheme.step: Waxy cuticle is waterproof and cuts water loss
Few stomata means less water vapour escapes

questions.stem_md: A leaf stalk is flexible while a coconut shell is hard. Name the tissue that explains each property and state one feature of its cells.

answer.model_answer_md: The leaf stalk is flexible because of collenchyma, whose living cells have thickened corners. The coconut shell is hard because of sclerenchyma, whose dead cells have very thick lignified walls.

questions.solution_md: Collenchyma for flexibility; sclerenchyma for hardness.

questions.stem_md: Name the three simple permanent tissues of plants. For each, state whether its cells are living or dead and give one job.

answer.model_answer_md: Parenchyma has living, thin-walled cells and it stores food, or makes food when it has chloroplasts. Collenchyma has living cells with thickened corners and gives flexible support. Sclerenchyma has dead cells with thick lignified walls and gives strength and hardness.

questions.solution_md: Parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma with state of cells and job.

marking_scheme.step: Parenchyma: living; stores or makes food

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled sketch of a plant showing where the three kinds of meristem lie.

(b) State two features of meristematic cells and the function of each kind of meristem.

answer.model_answer_md: The sketch shows the apical meristem at the shoot tip and root tip, the intercalary meristem at the base of a leaf or an internode, and the lateral meristem as a ring in the stem and root. Meristematic cells are small, thin-walled and closely packed, with dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus. They divide again and again. The apical meristem adds length at the tips, the intercalary meristem adds length at the base of leaves, as in grass, and the lateral meristem adds girth.

questions.solution_md: Sketch; two features; three functions.

marking_scheme.step: Labelled sketch with the three meristems
A function for each kind of meristem

questions.stem_md: Compare xylem and phloem in terms of the parts they contain, what they carry, the direction of movement and whether the cells are living or dead. Draw a labelled diagram of a phloem sieve tube with a companion cell.

answer.model_answer_md: Xylem contains vessels, tracheids, fibres and parenchyma, and it carries water and minerals upwards from the roots. Most of its cells are dead. Phloem contains sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres and parenchyma, and it carries food made in the leaves both upwards and downwards. Most of its cells are living. The diagram of the sieve tube shows the long tube with sieve plates across its ends and a thin companion cell beside it.

questions.solution_md: Four-point comparison and a labelled diagram.

marking_scheme.step: What each carries and in which direction
Diagram with sieve tube, sieve plate and companion cell

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

**(b)** The xylem in the wood is not cut, so water and minerals still reach the leaves.

questions.solution_md:

children.stem_md: The swelling just above the ring is most likely due to:

options.text_md: water collecting there because the xylem is cut
minerals from the roots collecting there because the phloem is intact
food from the leaves collecting there because it cannot pass the cut phloem
new leaves growing from the bark

children.solution_md: Food made in the leaves travels down through the phloem. The ring cuts the phloem, so food piles up above it and the bark swells — option (c).

children.stem_md: Why do the leaves above the ring stay green and fresh for some time?

answer.model_answer_md: The xylem in the wood is not cut, so water and minerals still reach the leaves.

marking_scheme.step: Xylem is intact and still carries water

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Predict what will happen to the part of the plant below the ring over many months, and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: The part below the ring will slowly weaken and die. Food made in the leaves cannot cross the cut phloem to reach it, so its cells, including the roots, run out of food for energy and growth.

children.solution_md: No food reaches the part below the ring.

marking_scheme.step: The part below the ring weakens and dies
Cut phloem stops food reaching it

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Suggest how the result would differ if the student removed a section of the wood (xylem) but left the bark, and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: The leaves above the cut would wilt and dry quickly, because without xylem water and minerals cannot reach them. The food made earlier could still move down through the intact phloem.

marking_scheme.step: Leaves wilt because water cannot rise

questions.stem_md: The cells that line the windpipe are tall and carry tiny hair-like projections that sweep mucus and dust upwards. This is:
questions.solution_md: Tall cells with cilia that sweep out mucus and dust are ciliated columnar epithelium — option (b). Squamous cells are flat, and cuboidal cells are cube-shaped.

questions.stem_md: A tissue has cells scattered in a liquid matrix and carries oxygen, food and wastes around the body. It is:
questions.solution_md: A liquid matrix, plasma, with cells that carry oxygen, food and wastes describes blood — option (b). Bone and cartilage have solid matrices, and adipose tissue stores fat.

questions.stem_md: A cell is long, with a cell body holding the nucleus and one long fibre that carries signals away. It belongs to:
questions.solution_md: A neuron has a cell body with a nucleus and a long axon that carries impulses away — option (d). Muscle cells contract instead of carrying signals.

questions.stem_md: A physiotherapist explains that a strong cord joins a footballer’s thigh muscle to a bone below the knee, and that a strong elastic band holds the thigh bone and the shin bone together at the knee. These two structures are, in that order:
questions.solution_md: A tendon joins muscle to bone and a ligament joins bone to bone, so the cord is a tendon and the band is a ligament — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A slide of muscle shows branched fibres with stripes, one nucleus in each cell and dark lines between neighbouring cells. Which statement about this muscle is correct?

options.text_md: It is found only in the heart and works without our control.
It is attached to bones and is under our control.
It forms the wall of the food pipe and has no stripes.
It has many nuclei at the edge and long unbranched fibres.

questions.solution_md: Striped, branched fibres with one nucleus are cardiac muscle, which is found only in the heart and is involuntary — option (a). The other options describe striated and smooth muscle.

questions.stem_md: In a neuron, the part that carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body towards other cells is the:
questions.solution_md: Dendrites receive signals and the axon carries the impulse away from the cell body — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A doctor explains that bone is hard but cartilage can bend. The hardness of bone is mainly due to its matrix, which contains:
questions.solution_md: Bone matrix is hard because of salts of calcium and phosphorus — option (d). Plasma is the matrix of blood and fat is stored in adipose tissue.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ligament joins a muscle to a bone.

**Reason (R):** A ligament is a strong and elastic band of connective tissue.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A ligament joins bone to bone, so A is false. R is a true description of a ligament — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Cardiac muscle shows light and dark stripes.

**Reason (R):** Cardiac muscle works without our control.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Cardiac muscle is striated, and it is involuntary, so both are true. But stripes are not a result of being involuntary, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Skeletal muscle shows light and dark stripes.

**Reason (R):** Skeletal muscle cells are spindle-shaped, with a single nucleus in the middle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Skeletal muscle is striated, so A is true. Its fibres are long and unbranched with many nuclei, and the spindle shape with one nucleus belongs to smooth muscle, so R is false — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A single neuron in the human body can be about a metre long.
questions.solution_md: True. The axon of a neuron that runs from the spinal cord to the foot can be about a metre long.

questions.stem_md: The strong, elastic band of connective tissue that joins one bone to another is called a ______.
questions.solution_md: A ligament joins bone to bone; a tendon joins muscle to bone.

questions.stem_md: The muscle found only in the wall of the heart is called ______ muscle.
questions.solution_md: Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary, and is found only in the heart.

questions.stem_md: The cardiac muscle of a boy contracts about 70 times a minute (illustrative value). About how many times does his heart contract in one full day of 24 hours?
questions.solution_md: Minutes in a day $= 60 \times 24 = 1440$. Contractions in a day $= 70 \times 1440 = 100800$. The heart muscle works all day without stopping, because it is involuntary and does not tire like other muscles.

marking_scheme.step: Finds the minutes in a day: 1440
Multiplies by the rate to get 100800

questions.stem_md: Bone and cartilage are both connective tissues. Give one difference in their matrix and one place where each is found.

answer.model_answer_md: The matrix of bone is hard because it contains calcium and phosphorus salts, and bone forms the skeleton, for example the thigh bone. The matrix of cartilage is firm but flexible, and cartilage is found in the nose, the ear and at the ends of bones in joints.

questions.solution_md: Hard against flexible matrix; skeleton against ear or nose.

marking_scheme.step: Bone: hard matrix; place such as the thigh bone
Cartilage: firm flexible matrix; place such as the ear

questions.stem_md: Why are the cells of the epithelium that lines the small intestine tall, while those lining a blood vessel are flat?

answer.model_answer_md: In the small intestine the cells are tall columnar cells, which have room to absorb food and secrete mucus. In a blood vessel the cells are thin and flat squamous cells, which let substances such as oxygen pass through them easily.

questions.solution_md: Tall cells absorb and secrete; flat cells allow exchange.

marking_scheme.step: Tall columnar cells: absorb food and secrete mucus
Flat squamous cells: easy exchange of substances

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between striated muscle and smooth muscle.

answer.model_answer_md: Striated muscle has light and dark stripes and many nuclei in each long fibre, whereas smooth muscle has no stripes and one nucleus in each spindle-shaped cell. Striated muscle is voluntary and attached to bones, while smooth muscle is involuntary and lines the food pipe.

questions.solution_md: Stripes and nuclei; control and place.

marking_scheme.step: Stripes and nuclei: present and many against absent and one
Voluntary against involuntary, with a place

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a neuron and say what each of its three main parts does.

answer.model_answer_md: A neuron has a cell body, branched dendrites and a long axon. The cell body holds the nucleus and keeps the cell alive. The dendrites receive signals and pass them to the cell body. The axon carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body, and nerve endings at its tip pass the signal on to the next cell.

questions.solution_md: Cell body, dendrites, axon, with jobs.

marking_scheme.step: Axon carries the impulse away to nerve endings

questions.stem_md: Connective tissue joins, supports and transports. Name five connective tissues and for each give one feature and one function.

answer.model_answer_md: Blood has cells in liquid plasma and transports oxygen, food and wastes. Bone has a hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus salts and supports and protects the body. Cartilage is firm and flexible and smooths joint surfaces and shapes the ear. A ligament is a strong elastic band that joins bone to bone. A tendon is a strong cord that joins muscle to bone, and adipose tissue stores fat as energy.

questions.solution_md: Five tissues with a feature and a function.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw labelled sketches of striated, smooth and cardiac muscle fibres.

(b) Compare the three kinds of muscle in a table that includes the stripes, number of nuclei, control and place in the body.

answer.model_answer_md: The sketches show striated fibres as long, unbranched and striped with many nuclei at the edge, smooth cells as spindle-shaped with no stripes and one central nucleus, and cardiac fibres as striped and branched with one nucleus. Striated muscle is voluntary and is found in the limbs and body wall. Smooth muscle is involuntary and is found in the food pipe and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and is found only in the heart.

questions.solution_md: Three sketches; four-point comparison.

children.stem_md: Slide R shows muscle from the:
children.solution_md: Striped, branched fibres with one nucleus and dark lines between cells are cardiac muscle, found in the heart — option (b).

answer.model_answer_md: Slide P, because it is striated muscle attached to bone, which is voluntary.

children.solution_md: P: striated and attached to bone.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Slide Q muscle moves food along the food pipe. Explain why it is useful that this muscle works involuntarily.

answer.model_answer_md: Food must be moved along by slow, steady squeezing, even when we are sleeping or thinking about something else. Because smooth muscle works involuntarily, digestion goes on without our having to give any thought or effort to it.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md: Meena touches the hot lid of a pressure cooker by mistake. In less than a second she pulls her hand away. Her teacher explains that tissues of four kinds took part: the skin of her finger, nerve cells that carried the signal to the spinal cord and back, a connective tissue that attaches her arm muscle to bone, and the muscle that contracted to pull the hand back.

children.stem_md: The cells that carried the signal from the finger to the spinal cord were:
children.solution_md: Neurons carry signals as nerve impulses — option (a). The other cells do not carry impulses.

children.stem_md: Name the connective tissue that joins the arm muscle to the bone.

answer.model_answer_md: The connective tissue that joins the arm muscle to the bone is a tendon.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain why a long axon is useful in a neuron that carries a signal from a finger to the spinal cord.

answer.model_answer_md: The finger is far from the spinal cord, so the cell must stretch the whole distance. A long axon carries the impulse along a single cell, which is quick, and it lets the signal reach its target without relay.

questions.stem_md: When you shake your head to say “no”, the first bone of the neck turns over the second bone. This movement happens at a:
questions.solution_md: Turning about an axis is the movement of a pivot joint, as in the neck — option (c). A hinge joint moves back and forth in one plane, and a fixed joint does not move.

questions.stem_md: A child who rarely goes out in the sun and eats very little milk or egg develops soft bones and bowed legs. The most likely cause is a shortage of:
questions.solution_md: Soft, bent bones in a growing child point to too little calcium and too little vitamin D, which helps absorb it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Kavya carries a heavy school bag on one shoulder all day and her back starts to ache. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text_md: Carry the bag on the other shoulder only.
Carry the bag on both shoulders, keep the load light and stand straight.
Sit very still all day so that the back can rest.
Take extra calcium tablets without changing anything else.

questions.solution_md: Sharing a lighter load across both shoulders and standing straight reduces the strain on the back and bones — option (b). Changing shoulders still leaves the load on one side, and extra tablets do not fix posture.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Children who get too little vitamin D may develop soft, bent bones.
